text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: NORA
text: Imagine you run a chain of restaurants with ten thousand employees. One morning your general counsel walks in and says a group of servers has filed a class action. They claim they were routinely asked to work through their breaks without pay. Not one server. All of them, across four years and two hundred locations.

speaker: JAMES
text: And the first question anyone asks is, how much? Is this a two hundred thousand dollar problem or a twenty million dollar problem? The answer is buried in millions of time punches, payroll records and schedules. And neither the lawyers nor the judge can do that maths in their heads.

speaker: NORA
text: So somebody has to. Somebody who can take that mountain of data, build a defensible estimate, and then stand up and explain it to a court while the other side's expert tries to take it apart.

speaker: JAMES
text: That somebody is often a labour economist. And today's company is a firm full of them.

speaker: NORA
text: Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time and look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'm James. Our series follows the companies in the portfolio of Levine Leichtman Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Beverly Hills. Last time it was Expert Institute, which helps lawyers find expert witnesses. Today it's Resolution Economics, a Los Angeles consultancy whose people often are the expert witnesses.

speaker: NORA
text: The usual note before we begin. Everything we discuss comes from public sources as of November 2026: company pages, press releases, trade press and the private equity firm's own announcements. When something is our opinion or an inference, we'll say so. And nothing in this episode is legal, employment or investment advice.

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd add one more note. This is a private firm that publishes very little about its size or finances. So there'll be a few places today where the honest answer is, we don't know.

speaker: NORA
text: Noted. So, James. Resolution Economics in one sentence.

speaker: JAMES
text: Resolution Economics, often shortened to ResEcon, is an economics, statistics and labour-economics consultancy that provides expert testimony and damages analysis in lawsuits, financial advisory work, digital forensics, workforce compliance services and, more recently, AI assurance, to law firms, corporations and employers.

speaker: NORA
text: That's a long sentence.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a broad firm. But if you want the short version, it's the people who do the numbers when employers end up in court, plus a growing business helping employers stay out of court in the first place.

speaker: NORA
text: And why is it interesting right now?

speaker: JAMES
text: Two reasons. First, it's one of three companies that its private equity owner moved into a continuation fund in late 2024, which gave it new money and more time. Second, it sells AI governance and bias testing to clients, which puts it right in the middle of one of the biggest questions in employment today. Can you trust an algorithm to help you hire, pay and promote people fairly?

speaker: NORA
text: Let's start with the basics. When was it founded and where?

speaker: JAMES
text: It was founded in 1998, according to both the private equity firm's page and the data provider CB Insights. It's headquartered in Century City in Los Angeles. And its offices, between its website and a December 2025 press release, now include Los Angeles, Downtown Los Angeles, Chicago, Washington, New York, Charlotte, Austin, Philadelphia, Morristown in New Jersey, Minneapolis and Toronto.

speaker: NORA
text: That's a lot of offices for a firm I'd never heard of.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a classic profile for this kind of firm. It's well known to employment lawyers and in-house legal teams, and almost invisible to everyone else. Consultancies like this grow through reputation inside a fairly small professional community.

speaker: NORA
text: Who runs it?

speaker: JAMES
text: The managing partner is Ali Saad, who holds a doctorate in economics. He's been a constant in the firm's public materials. J. Duross O'Bryan heads the Financial Advisory Services practice. Beth Ronnenburg is president of the Berkshire division, which we'll come to. And then there's a name that stands out. Victoria Lipnic leads what the firm calls its Human Capital Strategy Group. She's a former commissioner, and former acting chair, of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

speaker: NORA
text: Explain the EEOC for listeners outside the United States.

speaker: JAMES
text: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission is the federal agency that enforces American laws against workplace discrimination, on grounds like race, sex, age, disability and religion. Having someone who has led that agency on your team gives a firm real credibility when it advises employers on fairness, including the fairness of AI tools.

speaker: NORA
text: How big is ResEcon?

speaker: JAMES
text: We don't know. We didn't find a reliable headcount, revenue or client count anywhere public. The December 2025 release talks about six new offices and eight new partners that year, but it gives no totals. So I'm not going to guess.

speaker: NORA
text: What are the main practices?

speaker: JAMES
text: From the website, the main lines are labour and employment economics, financial advisory services including damages and valuation, digital forensics and electronic discovery, life sciences, an AI practice, and human resources compliance, which is largely the Berkshire division. That breadth is one of the firm's selling points. A law firm with a messy employment case can get the statistics, the data forensics and the damages work from one place.

speaker: NORA
text: You mentioned 2025 was a big year. What actually happened?

speaker: JAMES
text: The firm put out a release in December 2025 describing a year of significant growth and expansion. Six new offices, with Toronto, Austin and Morristown named, and eight new partners, including Tim Zimmerman and Rick Contorno in Toronto. It also said Janet Thornton, who holds a doctorate, joined the labour and employment practice. Earlier, in January 2025, it opened the Austin office in its financial advisory practice.

speaker: NORA
text: Eight partners in a year. Is that a lot?

speaker: JAMES
text: For a firm of this kind, I'd say it's a meaningful push, though without knowing the total number of partners it's hard to say how big a share it is. In consulting, partners are the engine. Each one brings expertise, a reputation and, often, client relationships. Hiring experienced partners from other firms, what the industry calls lateral hiring, is the fastest way to grow, and it's expensive. It fits with having fresh capital from the continuation fund.

speaker: NORA
text: And opening offices? In a world of video calls, does that still matter?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view it still does in this business. Lawyers like to work with experts they know, and local presence helps with that. Some court work is still very local. And a new office is often built around a partner who already has relationships in that city. So the offices and the partner hires are really the same strategy.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do the ownership history.

speaker: JAMES
text: In January 2020 Levine Leichtman acquired the firm, in its words, in partnership with management. We didn't find who the seller was. At the same time, CNL Strategic Capital, an investment vehicle, put in ten million dollars alongside the private equity firm's lower middle market fund.

speaker: NORA
text: So two investors at the start.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. And then at some later point, and we couldn't find the date, CNL sold its minority stake for about twenty-nine point two million dollars, according to CB Insights, to an entity owned by a Levine Leichtman affiliate and management, as part of a recapitalisation.

speaker: NORA
text: Ten million in, twenty-nine million out. That's a nice result for CNL.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is, on those reported numbers. It suggests the value of the business rose meaningfully in the years after 2020, although without the date and the exact terms I wouldn't push that too far.

speaker: NORA
text: And then the continuation fund. Explain what that is.

speaker: JAMES
text: Normally a private equity fund buys companies, holds them for a few years and sells them, and the fund has a fixed life. Sometimes the firm thinks a company still has a lot of growth ahead, but the original fund is reaching the end of its life. A continuation fund is a solution. The private equity firm sets up a new vehicle, brings in new investors, and the new vehicle buys the company from the old fund. Investors in the old fund can take their money out or roll into the new one.

speaker: NORA
text: So the owner effectively sells the company to itself.

speaker: JAMES
text: In a sense, yes, with new outside money and a fresh price set by the process. In November 2024 Levine Leichtman closed a five hundred and seventy-five million dollar multi-asset continuation fund, led by Hamilton Lane, a large investment firm. It moved three companies out of an older fund: Blue Ridge ESOP Associates, Milton Industries and Resolution Economics. The firm said the aim was to give those companies more time and additional capital to grow.

speaker: NORA
text: What does that mean for ResEcon in practice?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, two things. It has money for growth, which fits what we saw in 2025 with all the new offices and partners. And it has a new clock. The investors in the continuation fund will expect a return over the next few years, so the firm needs to show that its next phase of growth is real.

speaker: NORA
text: It's been owned by the same firm since January 2020. That's nearly seven years.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is, and that's why the continuation fund matters. A normal hold would probably have ended by now. This is a vote of confidence, but it also raises the bar.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about the core work. What does a labour economist actually do in a lawsuit?

speaker: JAMES
text: It depends on the type of case, but there are a few big ones. In a wage and hour class action, like our restaurant example, the question is how much unpaid time there was and what it's worth. In a discrimination case, the question might be whether women were paid less than men for comparable work, after accounting for legitimate factors like job, tenure and location. In a hiring case, whether a selection process screened out a protected group at a higher rate than you'd expect by chance.

speaker: NORA
text: So a lot of statistics.

speaker: JAMES
text: A lot of statistics, and a lot of data cleaning. Before you can run a single regression, you have to take payroll files, time clock data, human resources records and scheduling systems, often from different vendors and different years, and link them together. Employee IDs change. Job titles get renamed. A location closes. Half the effort is getting the data into a state where analysis is even possible.

speaker: NORA
text: Explain regression in a sentence for the non-statisticians.

speaker: JAMES
text: A regression is a way of estimating how much one thing, say pay, is associated with several other things at once, like experience, job level and location, so you can see whether a gap remains after accounting for the factors that legitimately explain it.

speaker: NORA
text: And then the economist testifies?

speaker: JAMES
text: Often, yes. Each side may have its own expert. The plaintiffs' economist might say the unpaid time is worth twenty million. The employer's economist might say the sampling was flawed and the real figure is two million. The judge, and sometimes a jury, has to weigh them. And there's another stage before that. In a class action, the court first has to decide whether the case can proceed as a class at all, and statistical evidence about whether the employees' experiences were similar enough often matters a lot there.

speaker: NORA
text: So the economist can shape whether there's a big case at all.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's exactly right, and it's why these firms are valuable. A strong analysis at the class certification stage can change the whole economics of a dispute. Many cases settle based on what those numbers show.

speaker: NORA
text: How do courts decide whether to trust an economist's method?

speaker: JAMES
text: As general background, American courts apply standards for expert evidence that ask, roughly, whether the method is reliable and whether it has been applied properly to the facts. Judges can exclude an expert whose analysis doesn't meet that bar. So a labour economist isn't just doing maths. They're doing maths that has to be explainable, replicable and defensible against a smart opponent who is trying to find the weak assumption.

speaker: NORA
text: Give me an example of a weak assumption.

speaker: JAMES
text: Suppose an economist estimates unpaid break time by looking at a sample of locations and extrapolating to all of them. If the sample isn't representative, maybe it over-weights the busiest restaurants, the estimate can be challenged. Or in a pay equity case, if the analysis leaves out a factor that genuinely explains pay, like shift differentials, the gap it finds may not be real. A good expert anticipates those attacks.

speaker: NORA
text: And pay equity is a growing area?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a significant one, as general background. Many states have strengthened pay equity laws in recent years, and some require pay ranges in job postings. Employers increasingly want to know, before anyone sues, whether they have unexplained pay gaps. That's work that sits right between ResEcon's litigation practice and its compliance practice.

speaker: NORA
text: And the financial advisory side?

speaker: JAMES
text: Broader commercial disputes. Damages from a broken contract, valuation of a business in a shareholder fight, lost profits after a supply failure. In January 2025 ResEcon opened an Austin office in that practice, led by partner Jeff Andrien with director Prateek Shah. And then there's digital forensics and e-discovery, which is about collecting and analysing electronic evidence like emails and system data.

speaker: NORA
text: It sounds like the common thread is data that matters in a dispute.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a very good way of putting it. Whether it's payroll records, financial statements or emails, the firm is in the business of turning messy data into evidence that can survive cross-examination.

speaker: NORA
text: Now the acquisitions. Under the private equity owner, ResEcon did three deals in fourteen months.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. In October 2022 it bought Berkshire Associates, based in Columbia, Maryland. Berkshire is a long-established firm that helps employers, especially federal contractors, with affirmative action plans, pay equity analysis and equal employment opportunity compliance. In November 2023 it bought the affirmative action, diversity and pay equity practices of Biddle Consulting Group, from Folsom, California, but not Biddle's testing product, TestGenius. And in December 2023 it bought The Red Maple Group, a small litigation economics firm from Oak Ridge, New Jersey, founded in 2018 with eight employees.

speaker: NORA
text: So two compliance deals and one litigation deal.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. Red Maple adds bench strength in the core litigation economics business. Berkshire and Biddle build a second engine, recurring compliance work for employers. That's an important strategic shift. Litigation is project by project and depends on case volume. Compliance work, by its nature, tends to recur every year. That second point is our inference about how those clients buy.

speaker: NORA
text: Now, I know our listeners who also follow our sister show will have heard a lot about Berkshire already.

speaker: JAMES
text: They will. Our sister podcast, Compliance Shift, has a full episode on Berkshire Associates called After the Mandate. It goes deep into Berkshire's history and what's happened to the federal affirmative action rules. So we'll keep it brief here and recommend that episode if you want the full story.

speaker: NORA
text: But give us the headline, because it matters for ResEcon as a whole.

speaker: JAMES
text: The headline, as general background, is that in January 2025 an executive order revoked the 1965 order that had required federal contractors to take affirmative action in employment and to keep written plans. The rules built on it have been rolled back since. A lot of Berkshire's traditional, recurring work was producing those plans. So a business ResEcon bought for its steady, recurring revenue has had part of its foundation removed.

speaker: NORA
text: That's a big deal.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is. Some obligations remain, for example around veterans and people with disabilities, which come from laws passed by Congress rather than an executive order, and employers still face legal risk on pay and hiring fairness. But the shape of the compliance business has changed. That's why I think ResEcon's AI governance and bias-testing work matters so much. It's partly a way to redeploy that compliance expertise toward where employer demand is heading.

speaker: NORA
text: And for the details, Compliance Shift, episode one.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's make the litigation work concrete. Take our restaurant chain from the cold open. An invented example, no real company.
chapter: A wage case, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. Let's call it Harbor Grill, two hundred locations, ten thousand hourly staff. Servers allege they were pressed to clock out for breaks and then keep working. Harbor Grill's outside law firm calls a labour economics consultancy, a firm like ResEcon, on the employer's side.
chapter: A wage case, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: What happens first?
chapter: A wage case, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Scoping. The economist sits down with the lawyers and asks: what's the class period, which job titles, which states, what's the theory of harm? Different states have different rules on breaks and overtime, so that changes the calculation. Then the data request. Four years of time punches, payroll, schedules, point-of-sale logins, maybe even security badge data.
chapter: A wage case, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Point-of-sale logins?
chapter: A wage case, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a clever check. If a server was clocked out for a break but was logged into the till entering orders, that's evidence of work during the break. Equally, if the logs show nobody touched the till during most breaks, that helps the employer.
chapter: A wage case, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Then the cleaning.
chapter: A wage case, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Then weeks of cleaning. The time clock system was replaced halfway through. Some locations used a different payroll vendor. Employee IDs were reissued. The team builds a single linked dataset of, say, forty million time punches and matches them to payroll and till activity.
chapter: A wage case, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And then the analysis.
chapter: A wage case, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: They measure how often breaks were short or missing, how often there was till activity during a recorded break, and how that varies across locations and managers. That last part matters a lot. If the problem is concentrated in a handful of locations with particular managers, the employer can argue that experiences weren't uniform enough for one big class. If it's everywhere, that points the other way.
chapter: A wage case, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And then the number.
chapter: A wage case, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: The economist builds damages estimates under different assumptions. If the plaintiffs' theory is right, here's the exposure. If only certain locations are affected, here's a smaller number. Those scenarios help the employer decide whether to fight, settle, or fix its practices quickly. And if it goes further, the economist writes a report, gets deposed, and may testify.
chapter: A wage case, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Where's the time going in that story?
chapter: A wage case, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: A huge share goes on the data work: understanding the systems, linking records, checking anomalies, rerunning analyses as the lawyers' theories change. That's skilled, billable work, and it's exactly the part where AI could change how many hours a case takes. Hold that thought for the AI section.
chapter: A wage case, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: How big is this market?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'll be cautious. IBISWorld, a market research firm, estimates the American expert witness consulting services industry at a bit under eight hundred million dollars in revenue, with nearly twelve thousand businesses. But the report is internally inconsistent about its dates, so I'd treat that as a very rough indication. We didn't find a reliable figure for the labour economics or human resources compliance niche specifically.

speaker: NORA
text: Nearly twelve thousand businesses. So it's fragmented.

speaker: JAMES
text: Very. Lots of small boutiques and individual experts, plus a set of larger, well-known economic consulting firms at the top. That fragmentation is one reason private equity likes these markets. There are plenty of smaller firms to buy, like Red Maple.

speaker: NORA
text: Who are the big names?

speaker: JAMES
text: Firms commonly listed as leaders in litigation and economic consulting include Analysis Group, Compass Lexecon, Cornerstone Research, The Brattle Group, NERA Economic Consulting and Berkeley Research Group, often called BRG. Those names come from an industry directory, and we didn't research their ownership or AI products, so I won't make claims about them beyond that they work in similar areas: damages, class actions, competition, securities and valuation.

speaker: NORA
text: And Expert Institute, from last week, appears on that list too.

speaker: JAMES
text: It does, but it's a different kind of competitor. Expert Institute helps lawyers find experts. ResEcon is the expert. In some cases, a law firm might use a service like Expert Institute to find an economist, and that economist could come from a firm like ResEcon or one of its rivals.

speaker: NORA
text: How does ResEcon differ from the big names?

speaker: JAMES
text: In our reading, the main point of difference is the combination of labour and employment economics with the human resources compliance business. The large firms listed don't advertise compliance services of that kind. So ResEcon can be in the courtroom when an employment dispute happens, and in the human resources department helping employers prevent the next one. That's our inference from their service menus, not something we've seen independently compared.

speaker: NORA
text: What drives demand?

speaker: JAMES
text: IBISWorld points to rising litigation volume and complexity, tighter financial regulation, and business expansion. In employment specifically, I'd add, as general background, that wage and hour class actions are a large and persistent feature of American litigation, and that AI in hiring is creating new questions about fairness that regulators and courts are only starting to answer.

speaker: NORA
text: And how do clients buy?

speaker: JAMES
text: In litigation, law firms and in-house counsel retain experts case by case, usually billed by the hour. In compliance, employers tend to buy on a recurring basis, typically annual. That's our inference about how the compliance side works. That mix of project and recurring revenue is part of the investment case.

speaker: NORA
text: How does a law firm actually choose which economist to hire?

speaker: JAMES
text: Mostly by reputation and track record, in our understanding. A partner at an employment defence firm will usually have a short list of experts they've used before and trust. They'll ask: has this person testified on this kind of case? Have they been excluded by a court? Are they good in a deposition? Are they conflicted with the other side? And can their team handle very large datasets quickly?

speaker: NORA
text: So it's a relationship business, much like Expert Institute's.

speaker: JAMES
text: Very much. But with one difference. Here the firm itself carries the reputation. When a law firm hires ResEcon, it's buying the credibility of a named partner and the reliability of the team behind them. That makes the brand of the individual expert very important, and it's why partner hiring and retention matters so much.

speaker: NORA
text: Does the speed of the team matter, or is it all about the name?

speaker: JAMES
text: Both. Litigation runs on deadlines. If the court wants an expert report in six weeks, and the data arrives late and messy, the team that can clean and analyse it fastest, without errors, is worth a lot. That's one of the places where, in my view, AI could become a genuine competitive weapon rather than just a cost saver.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk AI. There are two sides to this, aren't there? AI as something ResEcon sells, and AI as something ResEcon uses.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. On the selling side, the website lists four named AI services. AI governance. Bias and data quality assessment. AI development and validation. And AI litigation support.

speaker: NORA
text: Unpack those.

speaker: JAMES
text: AI governance is helping an organisation set up policies and controls for how it uses AI: who approves a model, how it's monitored, how decisions are documented. Bias and data quality assessment is testing whether an AI tool, say a resume screener or a pay recommendation model, produces unfair outcomes for particular groups, and whether the data it was trained on is sound. Development and validation is helping build or check models so they do what they claim. And litigation support is acting as experts when AI itself is the subject of a dispute.

speaker: NORA
text: What does a dispute about AI look like?

speaker: JAMES
text: Here are some invented examples. An applicant claims an AI screening tool rejected her because of her age. An employer and a software vendor argue over whether the vendor's model performed as promised. A company's pricing algorithm is accused of producing unfair outcomes for certain customers. In each case, someone has to examine the model, the data and the outcomes, and explain to a court what the system actually did.

speaker: NORA
text: And that's a statistics job as much as a computer science job.

speaker: JAMES
text: Often more so. The court doesn't usually need to know every line of code. It needs to know whether outcomes differed across groups, by how much, and why. That's the kind of question labour economists have been answering about human decision-makers for decades. I think that's a smart positioning, and in my view it could grow as more employment decisions run through software.

speaker: NORA
text: Why is a labour economics firm well placed for that?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because the statistical methods for testing whether a hiring process discriminates have been around for decades. Adverse impact analysis, comparing selection rates across groups, is bread-and-butter work for labour economists. An AI hiring tool is, in a sense, just a new selection process. The same questions apply. Does it screen out women, older workers or minority applicants at a higher rate, and if so, is that justified by the job?

speaker: NORA
text: And Victoria Lipnic's background helps there.

speaker: JAMES
text: Very much, in my view. A former acting chair of the EEOC on the team is a strong signal of credibility when an employer is deciding whose bias audit it trusts.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there regulation pushing this?

speaker: JAMES
text: As general background, yes, and it's patchy. New York City, for example, has a local law requiring bias audits for certain automated employment decision tools. Some states have passed or proposed laws on AI in hiring. And federal anti-discrimination law applies whether a decision is made by a person or an algorithm. I'd be careful about specifics, because the rules are shifting, but the direction is that employers need to be able to show their AI tools are fair.

speaker: NORA
text: Now the other side. Does ResEcon use AI internally?

speaker: JAMES
text: This is where the public record goes quiet. We didn't find any AI hires, AI partnerships, AI product launches or public statements about using AI in its own delivery. The AI services are just that, services, delivered by experts. We didn't find a software product. And we didn't see public evidence of AI built into its core workflows, like the data cleaning in our Harbor Grill example.

speaker: NORA
text: That doesn't mean it isn't happening.

speaker: JAMES
text: Correct. Many professional services firms use AI tools internally without announcing it. But from the outside, the honest summary is: ResEcon sells AI expertise to clients, and we can't see how much it's using AI on its own work.

speaker: NORA
text: Which is a bit like the cobbler's children.

speaker: JAMES
text: It might be, or it might just be quiet. Either way, I think the biggest AI opportunity for the firm is inside its own delivery model, and we'll get to that.

speaker: NORA
text: What about governance and security for the firm itself?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find published security certifications. For a firm that handles payroll and personnel data for large employers, and sensitive evidence in lawsuits, clients will ask about data protection. As with every company in this series, not seeing a certificate on a website doesn't mean it isn't there. But a firm that sells AI governance should, in my view, make its own governance very visible.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's list the challenges. What keeps leadership up at night, in your view?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd name five. First, concentration. From the practice mix, a big share of the work seems to be labour, employment and class action. If that market cools, or changes, the firm feels it. That's an inference, since we don't have revenue by practice.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, the people model. Like most consultancies, growth depends on hiring and keeping senior partners, the experts whose names appear on reports and who testify. The 2025 expansion, eight new partners and six new offices, shows it can recruit. But each partner is expensive, and if one leaves, clients may follow.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, the compliance shock we discussed. Part of the recurring revenue it bought through Berkshire and Biddle depended on federal rules that have changed. Rebuilding that business around what employers still need, pay equity, remaining obligations and AI fairness, is real work.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, integration. Three acquisitions in fourteen months, plus six new offices, means different systems, different cultures and different ways of working. Getting a Maryland compliance business, a California compliance practice, a New Jersey litigation boutique and a Los Angeles economics firm to work as one takes years.

speaker: NORA
text: And fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fifth, AI pressure on the billable hour. If AI makes data cleaning and analysis much faster, clients may expect fewer hours per case. That's good for clients and, if handled badly, bad for a firm that bills by the hour. It's the same tension we saw with BigHand's law firm customers.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a credibility risk too, using AI in expert work?

speaker: JAMES
text: A real one. An expert's analysis has to survive cross-examination. If an AI tool was used in the analysis, opposing counsel will ask how it works, whether it was validated, and whether the expert understands it. So any AI used in delivery has to be explainable and documented. Ironically, that's exactly what ResEcon advises its clients to do.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's turn to opportunities. If you were on the board, where would you push?

speaker: JAMES
text: First, AI-assisted data review and analysis in the core litigation work. Use AI to speed up the slow parts: understanding unfamiliar data systems, linking records, flagging anomalies, drafting first-pass summaries of documents. The aim is to cut analyst hours on large datasets and improve utilisation.

speaker: NORA
text: But if they bill by the hour, isn't that cutting their own revenue?

speaker: JAMES
text: In the short term it can be, which is why pricing matters. But there are ways it helps. Faster work can win more cases at the same headcount. Fixed-fee phases, for example a fixed price for the initial exposure analysis, can capture some of the efficiency as margin. And if a competitor gets faster first, clients will notice.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, productise the AI bias audit. Today it's sold as a service, engagement by engagement. Turning it into a recurring subscription, with a defined method, a regular schedule and a standard report, would create steady revenue that's less dependent on litigation cycles. text: I'd pull out four lessons. First, old skills can serve new markets. The statistics for testing whether a hiring process is fair have existed for decades. ResEcon has applied them to AI. Many firms have expertise that becomes newly valuable when a technology shift creates new questions.
